findings.where: Article page specimen, the pull quote (“Whichever PPP Law I am currently working on…”), compared with the hero's WRITE TO MARK button
findings.fault: The pull quote uses the same dovetail-handled tablet shape as the only button, at a larger size and with a heavier frame. The shape means "press me" in the hero and "read this quote" in an article. On an article page, where the quote is the only tablet in view, it becomes the strongest action-like shape on the screen, although clicking it does nothing (a false affordance).
findings.who_objects: A development-bank reader on one of Mark's articles, who learns from the homepage that the handled tablet is the way to reach Mark, then sees it around a quote and either tries it or stops trusting the shape. Angélique will add quotes to every new post, so the clash grows with the site.

findings.where: Hero headline (MARK · M · MOSELEY / INFRASTRUCTURE · ADVISOR), the article heading, the CINZEL specimen and the LAID · WEIGHTY · SETTLED motion title
findings.fault: Minium red is meant to be the one accent that leads to the action, but every display heading also uses it. On the first screen the two-line red headline sits right above the red button and outweighs it, so the colour that should say "this is the action" also says "this is a heading". Only the button's fill and handles set the action apart.
findings.who_objects: A first-time visitor deciding whether to get in touch, whose eye goes to the biggest red thing on the page (the name) and not to the one thing they can act on. The direction card's own rule (one accent, and it flows to the action) also objects.

findings.fault: LAY AGAIN is a button that replays the animation on the spot, but it is drawn with a link's underline, in the same treatment as the article's PDF link. It looks as if it would take the visitor somewhere else. The page's underline therefore means two functions.
findings.who_objects: Mark or the founder reviewing the tile, who wants to replay the arch-laying and may hold back from clicking something that looks like it leaves the page. The same pattern carried into the site would confuse readers who use the underline to spot links.
